project.name: Shop Checkout
project.description: A small e-commerce backend: a Next.js storefront, an Express orders API, BullMQ workers for payments and Redis Streams for notifications.

groups.name: AWS us-east-1
groups.description: Containers on ECS plus managed data stores.

nodes.name: Customer
nodes.summary: A shopper who browses the store and pays for an order.

nodes.name: Web App
nodes.summary: Next.js storefront that renders the catalog and the checkout page.
nodes.description:
The checkout page posts a form to a **server action** (`placeOrder`), so card details never touch our servers: the Stripe card element tokenizes them in the browser and only a `paymentMethodId` is sent.

The server action generates an `idempotency-key` per submit, which protects against double clicks and retries.

nodes.name: Orders API
nodes.summary: Express service that owns orders: creates them, queues payments and handles Stripe webhooks.
nodes.description:
The Orders API is the only writer of the `Order` table.

- `POST /orders` validates the cart, stores the order as `PENDING_PAYMENT` and enqueues a `payment.process` job. It answers `202 Accepted` right away; payment happens asynchronously.
- `POST /webhooks/stripe` verifies the Stripe signature, deduplicates events in Redis and confirms the order.

The webhook route uses `express.raw()` because signature verification needs the exact request bytes.

nodes.name: Postgres
nodes.summary: Primary database for orders and payment status.
nodes.description: Schema managed with Prisma. The `Order.status` column is the source of truth for the checkout state machine: `PENDING_PAYMENT` → `PAYMENT_PROCESSING` → `CONFIRMED` (or `FAILED`).

nodes.name: Redis
nodes.summary: Stores idempotency keys and processed Stripe event ids.
nodes.description:
Keys expire after 24 hours. `SET ... NX` makes the claim atomic, so two concurrent requests with the same key cannot both succeed.

The same Redis instance also backs the BullMQ payments queue and the `events:orders` stream.

nodes.name: Payments Queue
nodes.summary: BullMQ queue of payment jobs, retried with exponential backoff.
nodes.description: Each job carries the order id, amount, currency and Stripe payment method. Jobs are retried up to 5 times with exponential backoff starting at 2 seconds.

nodes.name: Payment Worker
nodes.summary: Consumes payment jobs and creates Stripe PaymentIntents.
nodes.description:
Runs up to 10 jobs concurrently. Uses `order-<id>` as the Stripe idempotency key, so a retried job never charges twice.

The worker only moves the order to `PAYMENT_PROCESSING`; the final confirmation comes from the Stripe webhook.

nodes.name: Notifications Worker
nodes.summary: Reads domain events from a Redis stream and sends transactional emails.
nodes.description: Uses a Redis Streams consumer group (`notifications`), so events are acknowledged only after the email is handed to the provider.

nodes.name: Stripe
nodes.summary: Payment processor: charges cards and reports results by webhook.

nodes.name: Email Service
nodes.summary: Postmark delivers transactional emails from templates.

edges.label: POST /orders
edges.description: Called from the `placeOrder` server action, with an `idempotency-key` header.

edges.label: SET NX
edges.description: Claims idempotency keys and Stripe event ids.

edges.label: POST /webhooks/stripe
edges.description: Signed with `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`; the route verifies it with `stripe.webhooks.constructEvent`.

edges.label: order.confirmed
edges.description: Published with `XADD` to the `events:orders` Redis stream and read by the `notifications` consumer group.

flows.name: Checkout
flows.summary: The customer pays for a cart. The order is stored, the payment is queued and a worker charges the card through Stripe.
flows.trigger: Customer clicks "Pay" on the checkout page

steps.title: Customer submits the checkout form
steps.description: Stripe Elements tokenizes the card in the browser, so only a `paymentMethodId` leaves the page.

steps.title: Server action calls POST /orders
steps.description: The request carries a fresh `idempotency-key`, so a double click cannot create two orders.

steps.title: API claims the idempotency key
steps.description: `SET idem:<key> 1 EX 86400 NX` succeeds only for the first request with this key. A duplicate gets `409 duplicate_request`.

steps.title: Payment job enqueued
steps.description: The API does not wait for the payment. BullMQ retries the job up to 5 times with exponential backoff.

steps.title: API answers 202 Accepted
steps.description: The web app redirects to the order page, which polls `GET /orders/:id` until the status changes.

steps.title: Payment worker picks up the job
Worker creates and confirms a PaymentIntent
steps.description: `order-<id>` is sent as the Stripe idempotency key, so a retried job never charges twice. The result arrives later by webhook.

flows.name: Stripe webhook → order confirmed
flows.summary: Stripe reports a successful payment. The API verifies the event, confirms the order and publishes order.confirmed.

steps.title: Stripe calls the webhook
steps.description: The API verifies the `stripe-signature` header against the raw request body.

steps.title: Event id deduplicated
steps.description: Stripe may deliver the same event more than once. A second delivery is acknowledged without side effects.

steps.title: API acknowledges with 200
steps.description: Any non-2xx answer makes Stripe retry the webhook with backoff for up to 3 days.

flows.name: Order confirmation email
flows.summary: The notifications worker turns order.confirmed into a templated email for the customer.
flows.trigger: An order.confirmed event lands on the events:orders stream

steps.title: Worker reads order.confirmed
steps.description: Read through the `notifications` consumer group with `XREADGROUP`.

steps.title: Worker loads the order and its items
Email sent with the order-confirmed template
steps.description: The stream entry is acknowledged (`XACK`) only after Postmark accepts the email, so a crash leads to a retry instead of a lost email.
